title: Adderall and Alcohol: Risks, Timing, and the Next-Day Crash
excerpt: Can you drink on Adderall? How the stimulant masks intoxication, why that leads to overdrinking, the strain on your heart, how long to wait, the next-day crash, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Is it safe to drink on Adderall? How the stimulant hides how drunk you are, strains your heart, how long to wait, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** mixing Adderall and alcohol is not a good idea, and most prescribers and pharmacists will tell you to avoid it or keep it to a minimum. The main danger isn't a chemical reaction between the two. It's that Adderall, a stimulant, hides how drunk you are. You feel more alert and in control than your blood alcohol level says you are, so it's easy to keep drinking well past the point where you'd normally stop. On top of that, both substances push on your heart, both dehydrate you, and the comedown the next day is usually worse than either one alone. This guide explains what actually happens in your body, how long to wait, what the next day looks like, and the warning signs that mean you should get help now.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink on the same day you take Adderall unless your prescriber has told you it's okay for you. If you do drink, have far less than you normally would, because you can't trust how you feel. Never take extra Adderall to "sober up" or to keep partying. Eat a real meal, drink water, and don't drink in hot, crowded places where you'll overheat. If someone has chest pain, a pounding or irregular heartbeat, a seizure, confusion, or can't be woken up, call **911** right away.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and drug-label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and your exact prescription. **Talk to your prescriber or pharmacist before drinking if** you take Adderall or any ADHD medication, especially if you have a heart condition, high blood pressure, anxiety, a history of seizures, or take antidepressants or other medicines. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** you or someone else has chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, a severe headache, a seizure, very high body temperature, confusion, or signs of alcohol poisoning such as vomiting while barely conscious, slow or irregular breathing, or being impossible to wake. In the US you can also call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222**.

## What Happens When You Mix Adderall and Alcohol

Adderall is a brand name for a mix of amphetamine salts (dextroamphetamine and amphetamine). It's a central nervous system stimulant. It works mainly by increasing the levels of two brain chemicals, dopamine and norepinephrine, which help with focus, attention, and alertness. Norepinephrine is also part of your body's "fight or flight" system, which is why Adderall raises heart rate and blood pressure.

Alcohol works in nearly the opposite direction. It's a depressant. It slows down brain activity, mainly by boosting the brain's main calming signal (GABA) and dampening its main excitatory signal (glutamate). That's what makes you relaxed, then clumsy, then sleepy as you drink more.

You might expect the two to cancel out. They don't. Each one keeps doing its own thing, and the combination creates problems neither causes alone.

### The masking effect: you feel less drunk than you are

This is the most important part of the whole topic. When you drink, the sleepiness and heaviness you feel are one of your body's built-in brakes. They're what tell you it's time to slow down or go home.

Adderall takes that brake off. The stimulant keeps you awake and alert, so you don't feel the usual drowsiness. But your blood alcohol level is exactly what it would have been without the Adderall. Your reaction time, judgment, coordination, and ability to drive are still impaired by the alcohol. You just can't feel it as clearly.

Researchers have described a similar pattern with energy drinks and alcohol, sometimes called being "wide-awake drunk." Lab studies giving people a stimulant with alcohol have generally found that the stimulant makes people *rate* themselves as less intoxicated, while tests of their actual performance still show the alcohol's effects. Adderall is a much stronger stimulant than the caffeine in an energy drink, so there's good reason to think the masking can be stronger.

What masking leads to in real life:

- **Drinking more than you planned.** If you don't feel drunk, you keep going.
- **Alcohol poisoning risk.** Drowsiness and passing out are, in a sense, protective. They stop you from drinking more. When a stimulant pushes back against them, people can reach dangerous blood alcohol levels while still standing.
- **Bad decisions that feel like good ones.** Driving, risky sex, fights, and accidents are all more likely when you feel sharper than you really are.
- **A sudden crash.** Adderall wears off on a schedule. Alcohol doesn't. When the stimulant fades, all the alcohol you've been drinking can hit you at once.

### Heart strain: two pushes in the same direction

Adderall raises heart rate and blood pressure. That's an expected, labeled effect, and it's why prescribers check for heart problems before starting it. The FDA prescribing information for amphetamine products warns about serious heart-related risks in people with existing heart disease or structural heart problems.

Alcohol also affects the heart. In the short term, drinking tends to raise heart rate, and heavy drinking can trigger abnormal heart rhythms. There's even a name for rhythm problems that show up after a binge, "holiday heart syndrome," most often involving an irregular rhythm called atrial fibrillation.

Put them together and your heart is getting pushed from two sides at once. For most young, healthy people, a small amount of each won't cause a cardiac emergency. But the risk climbs with higher doses of Adderall, more alcohol, dehydration, heat, dancing for hours, and any underlying heart condition, which some people don't know they have. If you've ever felt your heart pounding after drinking, our guide on [why your heart races after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains that side of it.

### Dehydration and overheating

Alcohol makes you pee more by suppressing a hormone (vasopressin) that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. Amphetamines can raise body temperature and make you sweat, and they also blunt thirst and hunger. In a hot bar or a packed party, that combination can leave you dehydrated and overheated without noticing.

### Empty stomach

Adderall is well known for killing appetite. Many people on it barely eat during the day. Drinking on an empty stomach lets alcohol reach your bloodstream faster, so your blood alcohol level rises more steeply. Now combine that with the masking effect: you get drunker faster and feel it less.

### Mood, anxiety, and the comedown

As Adderall wears off, many people feel a "crash": tired, irritable, low, or anxious. Alcohol is a depressant, and the day after drinking often brings its own anxiety (often called "hangxiety"). Stacking the stimulant comedown on top of an alcohol hangover can make the next day feel noticeably worse mentally. For people who already deal with anxiety or depression, which is common alongside ADHD, this is worth taking seriously.

## Can You Drink on Adderall?

There's no single answer that applies to everyone, which is exactly why this is a conversation to have with your prescriber. What can be said generally:

- **The safest choice is not to drink on days you take Adderall.** That's the standard advice you'll hear from most pharmacists.
- **Some prescribers are comfortable with occasional light drinking** for certain patients, for example a single drink with dinner well after a morning dose has worn off. That's a judgment call based on your dose, your health, and your history. Ask rather than guess.
- **Heavy drinking or binge drinking on Adderall is where the real danger is.** The masking effect, heart strain, and alcohol poisoning risk all scale with how much you drink.
- **Don't skip or change your dose on your own** so you can drink. Ask your prescriber how to handle it. Some people are told it's fine to skip a dose on a weekend, others are not, and it depends on why you take the medication.

One more point worth stating plainly. Adderall is a Schedule II controlled substance, and its FDA label carries a boxed warning (the strongest kind) about misuse, abuse, and addiction. Taking someone else's Adderall, or taking more than prescribed, to party or to drink longer is both riskier and illegal. Surveys of college students have repeatedly found that people who use prescription stimulants without a prescription are more likely to binge drink, and that combination is where many of the worst outcomes happen.

## How Long After Taking Adderall Can You Drink?

There's no official waiting period, and anyone who gives you an exact number of hours for everyone is guessing. What helps is knowing how long the drug lasts.

| Version | Typical duration of effect | What it means for drinking |
|---|---|---|
| Adderall (immediate release) | About 4 to 6 hours per dose | If you took a morning dose, the main effect is usually fading by late afternoon, but the drug is still in your system longer. |
| Adderall XR (extended release) | Up to about 10 to 12 hours | A morning dose can still be active into the evening, right when people tend to drink. |

A few things to keep in mind:

- **"Worn off" isn't the same as "gone."** Amphetamine stays in your body well after you stop feeling it. Its half-life (the time it takes for half of it to leave your body) is roughly 10 hours in adults, and it varies from person to person.
- **The later and bigger your dose, the more overlap.** A late-afternoon dose of XR overlaps heavily with an evening of drinking.
- **Ask your prescriber about your specific dose.** They can tell you whether waiting until evening is enough for you, or whether it's better to skip drinking that day.

If you know you'll be drinking, a practical approach many people discuss with their doctor is simply planning ahead: deciding in advance whether to take the dose that day, and how much they'll drink, rather than figuring it out at the bar.

## Taking Adderall After Drinking (or Mid-Night)

Some people take Adderall during a night out to stay awake, or the next morning to push through a hangover. Neither is a good idea.

- **Mid-night doses make the masking worse.** You'll feel more alert, drink more, and stay up later. Your heart takes the extra load and your sleep gets wrecked.
- **The morning after, your body is already strained.** You're likely dehydrated, short on sleep, and your heart rate may still be up. Adding a stimulant on top can make a racing heart, shakiness, and anxiety worse.
- **If you take Adderall as prescribed every morning,** don't double up or take extra because you feel rough. Take your normal dose only if your prescriber has said that's fine after a night of drinking, eat breakfast, and drink water. If you feel unwell, it's reasonable to call your pharmacist and ask.

## The Adderall Hangover: What the Next Day Looks Like

Mixing the two often produces a next day that's worse than a normal hangover. Common complaints include:

- **Poor or almost no sleep.** Adderall keeps you awake, and alcohol breaks up sleep later in the night even if it helps you nod off. Together they can leave you running on a couple of hours. Our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains the alcohol side of this.
- **A deeper crash.** Stimulant comedown fatigue plus hangover fatigue.
- **Stronger anxiety and low mood.** Both the stimulant wearing off and the alcohol leaving your system can bring on anxiety. See our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) for more.
- **Dehydration symptoms.** Headache, dry mouth, dizziness when you stand up.
- **Not eating.** Appetite suppression carries into the next day for some people, which makes recovery slower.
- **A pounding heart or shakiness**, especially if you also had a lot of caffeine.

### What actually helps

There's no trick that cancels this out. The basics work best:

1. **Drink water steadily** through the day. An electrolyte drink can help if you've been sweating or vomiting.
2. **Eat something,** even if you're not hungry. Plain carbs and some protein are easiest.
3. **Skip extra caffeine** if your heart is already racing.
4. **Rest.** Let yourself sleep if you can.
5. **Don't use more stimulants** to push through.
6. **Be careful with painkillers.** If you need one, follow the label, take it with food, and check with a pharmacist if you're unsure which one fits your situation.

Most of this clears within a day. If you still feel very unwell after that, or your heart symptoms don't settle, get checked.

## Does This Apply to Other ADHD Medications?

The same broad logic applies to the other stimulants, though the details differ.

- **Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine)** is a long-acting amphetamine-type medication. The masking effect and heart strain are similar, and because it lasts most of the day, the overlap with evening drinking is larger.
- **Ritalin, Concerta, and Focalin (methylphenidate and dexmethylphenidate)** are a different stimulant family, but they also raise heart rate and blood pressure and can mask intoxication. Research has also found that when methylphenidate and alcohol are taken together, the body forms a compound called ethylphenidate and the level of methylphenidate in the blood can rise. That's one more reason to avoid combining them.
- **Non-stimulant options such as Strattera (atomoxetine), Qelbree (viloxazine), or guanfacine** work differently and don't produce the same stimulant masking effect, but they have their own interactions and side effects. Guanfacine, for example, lowers blood pressure and can make you drowsy, which alcohol can intensify. Ask your prescriber about the one you take.

For any ADHD medication, the rule is the same: check with the person who prescribed it, using your exact drug and dose.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from combining Adderall and alcohol if you:

- Have **any heart condition**, high blood pressure, or a family history of sudden cardiac death or heart rhythm problems
- Take a **higher dose** or the **extended-release** version
- Have **anxiety, panic attacks, depression, or bipolar disorder**
- Have a **history of seizures**
- Take **other medicines** that affect mood, heart rate, or blood pressure, including some antidepressants
- Tend to **binge drink** or drink quickly
- Are using Adderall **without a prescription** or at a higher dose than prescribed
- Are drinking in **hot, crowded settings** where you'll be dancing or active for hours

If any of these describe you, the safer default is not to drink on Adderall days, and to talk it through with your doctor. For a broader look at how common medicines interact with alcohol and supplements, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

Most people who mix a normal dose with a drink or two will just feel off. But the combination can turn serious, and the masking effect means people sometimes don't realize how much trouble they're in. Don't wait it out if you see these.

**Call 911 or go to the emergency room for:**

- Chest pain or pressure
- A very fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle with rest
- Fainting, or feeling like you're about to faint
- A sudden, severe headache, or trouble speaking, weakness on one side, or vision changes
- A seizure
- Very high body temperature, hot dry skin, or confusion
- Severe agitation, paranoia, or seeing or hearing things that aren't there

**Signs of alcohol poisoning (also call 911):**

- Can't be woken up, or keeps drifting out of consciousness
- Slow breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or long gaps between breaths
- Vomiting while confused or barely conscious
- Pale, blue-tinged, or cold, clammy skin
- Low body temperature

If someone is passed out, roll them onto their side so they won't choke if they vomit, and stay with them until help arrives. Don't try to "wake them up" with more stimulants, coffee, or a cold shower. Tell the paramedics about every substance involved, including the Adderall. They're there to help, not to judge, and that information changes how they treat someone.

## Talking to Your Doctor About Drinking

A lot of people avoid bringing up alcohol with the doctor who prescribes their ADHD medication. That's understandable but it works against you. Prescribers hear this question all the time, and an honest conversation gets you advice that actually fits your life.

Useful questions to ask:

- "Is it okay for me to have a drink on days I take my medication? If so, how much and how long after my dose?"
- "Should I skip my dose on days I plan to drink, or is that a bad idea for me?"
- "Given my heart health and blood pressure, are there extra risks for me?"
- "Are any of my other medications a problem with alcohol?"

If you find that you're regularly using Adderall to drink more, or drinking to come down from Adderall, that's worth raising too. Your doctor can help you adjust the plan.

## Where Supplements Fit (and Where They Don't)

No supplement makes it safe to combine Adderall and alcohol. Nothing removes the masking effect, protects your heart from the double push, or lowers your blood alcohol level faster. The steps that really help are drinking less, drinking slower, eating, hydrating, and not drinking at all on days when the overlap is large. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people ask about **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, with only a small amount of human data. There is no good evidence on how DHM interacts with Adderall or other ADHD medications, and it does nothing to reverse the stimulant's masking effect. If you take a prescription stimulant, ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement, DHM included.

If your doctor is comfortable with you having the occasional drink and you want to try DHM on those nights, a simple, low-cost option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Treat it as an extra at most, never as a reason to drink more on Adderall.

## The Bottom Line

- Adderall doesn't lower your blood alcohol level. It hides how drunk you are, which makes overdrinking and alcohol poisoning more likely.
- Both substances raise heart rate and strain the heart, and the risk climbs with higher doses, more drinks, heat, and dehydration.
- The safest choice is not to drink on days you take Adderall. If you want to drink sometimes, ask your prescriber how to do it for your dose.
- Extended-release versions can still be active into the evening, so "I took it this morning" doesn't mean it's gone.
- Never take extra Adderall to stay out longer or to push through a hangover.
- Chest pain, an irregular heartbeat, a seizure, confusion, overheating, or signs of alcohol poisoning mean call 911 now.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is it dangerous to mix Adderall and alcohol?**

It can be. The biggest risk is that Adderall hides how drunk you feel, so you may drink much more than you normally would and reach dangerous blood alcohol levels. Both substances also raise heart rate and can strain the heart, and the next-day crash tends to be worse. Small amounts are less risky than heavy drinking, but most prescribers advise avoiding or keeping alcohol to a minimum on days you take Adderall. Ask your prescriber what's safe for you.

**How long after taking Adderall can I drink?**

There's no official waiting period. Immediate-release Adderall usually lasts about 4 to 6 hours, and Adderall XR can last up to about 10 to 12 hours, but the drug stays in your system longer than you feel it. A morning dose of the extended-release version can still overlap with evening drinking. Ask your prescriber about your specific dose and timing.

**Can you get drunk faster on Adderall?**

Adderall doesn't make alcohol stronger, but it changes how drunk you feel. Because it suppresses appetite, many people drink on an empty stomach, which makes blood alcohol rise faster. At the same time, the stimulant hides the drowsiness that normally warns you to slow down. The result is that people often get drunker than they realize.

**Why does Adderall make me feel sober when I'm drinking?**

Adderall is a stimulant that increases alertness. It pushes back against the sleepiness and sluggishness alcohol causes, so you feel more awake. But your blood alcohol level, reaction time, coordination, and judgment are still affected by the alcohol. Feeling sober isn't the same as being sober, and you should never drive after drinking, whether or not you took Adderall.

**What is an Adderall hangover?**

It's the rough next day many people get after combining Adderall and alcohol. It usually involves poor sleep, a heavy crash as the stimulant wears off, stronger anxiety or low mood, dehydration symptoms like headache and dizziness, and sometimes a racing heart. Water, food, rest, and avoiding extra caffeine or stimulants help most. If heart symptoms don't settle, get checked.

**Should I skip my Adderall dose if I'm going to drink?**

Don't decide this on your own. For some people a prescriber is fine with skipping a dose on a day they plan to drink, and for others that's not a good idea, depending on why they take the medication. Ask your prescriber ahead of time so you have a plan rather than figuring it out on the night.

**Is it safe to take Adderall the morning after drinking?**

If you take Adderall daily as prescribed, ask your prescriber whether to take your normal dose after a night of drinking. Never take extra to push through a hangover. Your body is often dehydrated and short on sleep, and adding a stimulant can make a racing heart, shakiness, and anxiety worse. Eat, drink water, and call your pharmacist if you feel unwell.

**What are the signs of an emergency after mixing Adderall and alcohol?**

Call 911 for chest pain, a very fast or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, fainting, a seizure, a severe headache, overheating or confusion, or severe agitation or paranoia. Signs of alcohol poisoning also need emergency care: not being able to wake someone, slow or irregular breathing, vomiting while barely conscious, or pale, blue-tinged, cold skin. Tell responders about every substance involved.

**Does DHM make it safe to drink on Adderall?**

No. There is no good evidence on how DHM interacts with Adderall, and it does not reverse the stimulant's masking effect or protect your heart. DHM has some promising research on alcohol metabolism, mostly from animal studies with limited human data. If you take a prescription stimulant, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.
